Treat as a nursery/lookalike comparison: pinnate evergreen leaves with many holly-like leaflets and blue-purple berry clusters. It is not native to Texas under the current Kew concept.

Low annual with axillary flower clusters from base to top; the cluster axes become thick, inflated and hard at maturity, with uniquely keeled flower bracts.
Start with the compound leaf: many narrow lance-shaped leaflets sit along a conspicuously winged rachis. Then confirm the deciduous, clonal shrub/small-tree habit and vivid red fall color.

Look for a low, densely hairy plant with dark maroon-to-brown star-shaped flowers, commonly paired close to the stem and heart-shaped leaves. Then inspect the milkweed gynostegium in the flower center.
Look for a vigorous twining vine with large opposite cordate leaves, relatively large uniform olive-green star-shaped flowers, and a long smooth follicle with strong longitudinal angles.

Like Texas snakeweed, an open and wispy yellow-flowering annual. Examine the back of a real flower head: pale/resinous phyllaries without green midnerve borders; then the DISC floret has long white basally united pappus scales, unlike G. texana's nearly absent/very short scales.

Start with life cycle, foliage, and ray pattern. Rock tickseed is an annual with narrow linear leaves and slender branching stems; the yellow ray florets usually carry rusty-red/brown color at the base.

Expect an intermediate ironweed. Plants occur where western ironweed and woolly ironweed meet, with foliage, hairiness, leaf width, and head characters falling between the parents.
Yellow-flowered bladderpod whose upper leaves are notably sessile, helping separate it from more obviously petiolate relatives.

Find an areole before anything else. On the flattened green cladodes, each areole is a specialized short shoot that can carry hairs, glochids, permanent spines, flowers, or new pads. Then compare pad shape, spine/glochid pattern, yellow-to-orange flower, and beet-red berry.

Compare the whole plant against Texas pricklypear before counting spines. O. macrorhiza is usually a low, sprawling grassland cactus with smaller pads close to the ground. Then check the areoles: relatively few permanent spines, often with the main spine strongly bent or deflexed

Low gray prairie subshrub with densely silky compound leaves and narrow upright violet-purple flower spikes.
Texas annual milkvetch in the Nuttallianus complex with 4–12 flowers per raceme, relatively broad leaflets, and long narrow glabrous pods.
Compare leaf breadth, lower-surface pubescence, acorn shape, geography, and Q. fusiformis overlap. Ambiguous Central Texas live oaks should remain unresolved.

Start with the fluffy head. Bushy bluestem makes dense broomlike to cottony clusters near the top of the plant, with paired short rames packed inside and emerging from upper leaf sheaths. The inflorescence looks bushy rather than like separate turkey-foot fingers.

Check the stem nodes before the seedhead. Cane bluestem has a conspicuous dense beard/ring of soft hairs around the node, often several millimeters long. Then confirm the fanlike silvery panicle: many primary branches spread nearly as long as the main inflorescence.

Annual habit + coarse many-flowered spikelets + crater-like glands on panicle branches, pedicels, glumes or lemma keels.

Start at the panicle and sheath collar. Plains lovegrass is a tufted perennial with an extremely open, airy panicle whose tiny spikelets sit on long divergent pedicels. Leaf sheaths are mostly glabrous, with hairs concentrated near the sheath apex/collar rather than being shaggy
Look for a tufted perennial lovegrass with very narrow, firm, inward-rolled leaves and a comparatively restrained panicle rather than the broad airy cloud of purple lovegrass.
Look for dense clusters of spikelets packed along the panicle branches. The spikelets often become violet to reddish, giving the inflorescence a heavier, chunkier look than purple lovegrass.
Ignore the old Panicum label and look at the runners: long wiry stolons with swollen woolly nodes root to make new plants, while narrow upright seedheads rise from the sod.

Forget the ornamental-muhly silhouette: nimblewill is low and weak. Look for decumbent much-branched stems that root at the lower nodes, short flat blades, and a narrow contracted panicle. That creeping/rooting habit separates it instantly from the two upright bunchgrasses.

Think intermediate between Lindheimer muhly and seep muhly: a dense upright perennial bunchgrass with firm folded leaves and an open erect panicle, usually in rocky canyons and prairie openings where the parent ranges overlap.
Look for hair plus chaos: witchgrass is an annual with conspicuously hairy sheaths/nodes and an enormous, extremely open many-branched panicle that can look like a tumbleweed.
Small Texas fluffgrass relative with a compact seedhead and conspicuous cottony or fluffy hairs around the spikelets at maturity.

Look at the flowering spike before anything else: a thick corn-relative spike has male spikelets on the upper portion and hard bead-like female spikelets below, all rising from a huge broad-leaved rhizomatous clump.

Look for the gray cast before anything else: this is the short, low vervain whose stems and leaves are densely covered in stiff whitish hairs, giving the entire plant a canescent or dusty-gray appearance.
